The host can be templated too (`https://:tenant.example.com/api`). A placeholder in the authority whose name is only digits is treated as the port and is left unchanged, and the colons inside an IPv6 literal such as `http://[2001:db8::1]/api` are part of the address rather than placeholders. A value substituted into the authority is **not** escaped — a `%XX` below `0x80` inside a host makes the URL parser discard the rest of the URL — so it must already be a valid host: unreserved characters, `$`, `&`, `+`, `=` and valid UTF-8 for an IDN label. Malformed UTF-8 is rejected too — the bytes reach the `Host` header verbatim, and an overlong sequence such as `%C0%AF` is a `/` to a lenient decoder. Anything else, including a `:` or `@` that would add a port or a userinfo section and send the request to another host, fails the request with `ErrPathParamInHost`. A port can still be templated by giving the placeholder a name that is not all digits, as in `https://example.com::port/api`.

`SetDisablePathNormalizing(true)` on the client or request turns that check off for `/` and `\`, but only for a client that Fiber knows sends the path as built: one whose wrapped fasthttp client has path normalizing turned off and has not served a host while it was on. [SetDisablePathNormalizing](./rest.md#setdisablepathnormalizing) on the client does that for a client from `New`, `NewWithHostClient` or `NewWithLBClient`. A `fasthttp.Client` given to [NewWithClient](./rest.md#newwithclient) may have served hosts already and Fiber cannot tell, so it counts only when it was created with `DisablePathNormalizing: true`. Nothing decodes the path afterwards then, a `/` in a value is emitted as `%2F` and the value is sent as one segment. Whether it stays one segment is up to the server — one that unescapes paths, including a Fiber server configured with `UnescapePath`, decodes it again while routing. On any other client the check stays on, whatever the client or the request asks for, so a value such as `x/../../admin` is rejected rather than changing the path that is sent. The values the setting never lets through are `.` and `..`, which would go out as dot segments that the receiving server resolves, and an empty value, which leaves a `//` that a server merging slashes drops: no escape keeps them in place. Each of them followed by `;` parameters, such as `..;`, stays rejected as well. A `?` or `#` in a value is always contained; normalizing does not decode those.

### SetDisablePathNormalizing

Turns path normalizing off or on for every request of the client. It is on by default: the request path is normalized before it is sent, which decodes percent-escapes, collapses `//` and resolves `.` and `..` segments, so `/a//b/./c%2Fd` goes out as `/a/b/c/d`. With normalizing off, the path is sent as written. fasthttp normalizes the path when it writes the request, according to the client that sends it, so the setting is applied to the `DisablePathNormalizing` field of the wrapped fasthttp client, and of every host client behind a load balancer: a client created with [NewWithClient](#newwithclient), [NewWithHostClient](#newwithhostclient) or [NewWithLBClient](#newwithlbclient) changes the fasthttp client it wraps, for everyone who shares it. Call it before the first request, because a `fasthttp.Client` copies the setting into each host client when it first creates it, and a host it already serves keeps normalizing until fasthttp drops its entry, see the note under [TLS](#tls) for when. Fiber keeps rejecting path parameter values that would leave their segment unless it knows that the path is sent as built. It knows for a client from `New`, until a request has gone out through it while it normalized; for a client from `NewWithHostClient`, which reads the field on every request; for a client from `NewWithLBClient` whose host clients all have the field on; and for a `fasthttp.Client` given to `NewWithClient` that was created with `DisablePathNormalizing: true`. A `fasthttp.Client` given to `NewWithClient` without it may have served hosts already, so Fiber cannot tell and keeps the check on, although hosts it has not served yet get the setting. A balancer that holds a client that is neither a `*fasthttp.HostClient` nor a wrapper exposing a nested balancer through `LBClient()` cannot be told either and counts as normalizing. A request skips Fiber's normalizing when either the client or the request disables it; see [SetDisablePathNormalizing](./request.md#setdisablepathnormalizing) for the request-level setting.

```go title="Signature"
func (c *Client) SetDisablePathNormalizing(disable bool) *Client
```
